render.title: Cytochrome c oxidase reaction products
render.summary: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) passes four electrons to one oxygen molecule, producing two water molecules and pumping four protons.
render.body:
Complex IV, also called cytochrome c oxidase, is the final protein complex in the electron transport chain. It receives electrons from cytochrome c, a small mobile protein that ferries electrons from Complex III, and uses them to reduce molecular oxygen to water.

How the electron transfer works:

Cytochrome c carries one electron at a time and docks onto the intermembrane-space face of Complex IV. The complex contains several metal centres, including copper ions (the CuA centre) and haem groups (haem a and haem a3), as well as a second copper site (CuB). Electrons pass from cytochrome c into the CuA centre, then along the internal metal chain to haem a3 and CuB, which together form the active site where oxygen binds.

The oxygen reduction step:

One molecule of oxygen (O2) requires four electrons to be fully reduced. Complex IV collects these four electrons sequentially from four separate cytochrome c molecules. The reaction at the active site is:

O2 + 4 electrons + 4 protons (from the matrix) → 2 H2O

So two water molecules are produced for every oxygen molecule reduced. These water molecules are released into the mitochondrial matrix.

Proton pumping:

At the same time, Complex IV uses the energy released by this electron transfer to pump four additional protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, from the matrix side to the intermembrane space. This adds to the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.

In total, for every O2 molecule reduced:
- 4 protons are consumed from the matrix to make water
- 4 protons are pumped into the intermembrane space

This dual use of protons (as chemical reactants for water and as pumped ions for the gradient) makes Complex IV a particularly efficient link in the energy conversion chain.

Why this step matters:

Without Complex IV accepting electrons from cytochrome c and passing them to oxygen, the entire chain would back up. Electrons would have nowhere to go, proton pumping at Complexes I and III would stop, the gradient would collapse, and ATP synthesis would halt. Oxygen is not just a fuel but the essential electron sink that keeps the whole process running.
render.canonical_question: At the terminus of the respiratory chain, how does cytochrome c oxidase reduce molecular oxygen, how many protons does it translocate, and what metabolite is formed?
seeds: What happens to the electrons in cytochrome c oxidase if a molecule like cyanide blocks the haem a3 active site?
Why must Complex IV collect four electrons before it can reduce oxygen, rather than reducing it two electrons at a time?
How do the protons used to make water differ from the protons that are pumped across the membrane?
